skip.battery_stopped: Not tested: the battery was stopped for temperature.
skip.expired: Not finished: the published action ran out.
skip.no_baseline: Not proven: the battery was already doing what this action asks, so a change can't be seen.

**Debug file created**

1. Download it: {download} (the link works for {hours} hours, the file is also saved as `{file}` in the config folder).
2. [Open a GitHub issue]({issue}) - the version and the time are filled in.
3. Describe what happened, when it happened and what you expected, and drag the file into the field *Debug file*.

Create the file as soon as possible after the problem: it holds the latest calculations and log messages.

The file contains your settings, prices, energy history and plans, the blueprint automations and the integrations and device models you use. dashboard.what_if_baseline_note: Current is an estimate: the simulation assumes the current configuration was used throughout the period. Focus especially on the difference between current and scenario; that difference is also an estimate.
dashboard.what_if_dashboard_help: Compare what the battery would have saved, with different sizes and settings, using your own history. Results are historical estimates, not a guarantee for the future: the simulation knows the actual consumption and solar production in advance, so real results are usually somewhat lower. Annual gain and payback need a 365-day period; missing hours are estimated from the same or the nearest month. Module prices do not include installation.
dashboard.what_if_module_baseline_note: The zero-module baseline is simulated at current capacity using the same assumptions as each added-module case.
dashboard.what_if_module_coverage_requirement: Annual gain and payback need a 365-day period (*History (days)* = 365) with at least about half of it in Home Assistant's history, and known historical sell prices and costs. A shorter period is not scaled up to a year.

dashboard.what_if_module_monthly_title: Monthly breakdown: Current, scenario and difference
dashboard.what_if_module_monthly_note: Gain per calendar month in the selected period, so you can see when in the year it pays most. This is not a forecast; months with few hours are incomplete. Bold marks the best month.
dashboard.what_if_module_payback_title: Payback over time: electricity bill and battery purchase
dashboard.what_if_module_payback_note: The chart shows the total cost over time with an unchanged yearly bill. The grey line is without a battery. The other lines start at the purchase price of the battery size in the legend and rise with the bill for that size. The dot shows when the whole battery has paid for itself against no battery at all; the legend also shows how long the last module alone takes. The chart shows at most 30 years. It is an estimate from the history and excludes installation, financing, taxes and future changes. The current battery is priced at the same price per kWh as a module.

dashboard.what_if_module_summary_total: The whole {capacity} kWh battery against no battery at all pays back after {time}. That is faster than the extra kWh alone because your current battery pays back faster and pulls the average down. The figure applies as if you bought the whole battery today.

dashboard.what_if_module_summary_advice: If you are thinking of buying more, use the time for the extra kWh alone: your current battery is already bought. All figures are historical estimates, not guarantees.

Results are historical estimates, not guarantees.

dashboard.what_if_interval_chart: Profit change per added kWh of battery capacity
dashboard.what_if_interval_example: Each point shows the profit per added kWh for the interval below it. For example, 8–16 compares a 16 kWh battery with an 8 kWh battery. A negative value means the larger battery produced less profit during the period.
dashboard.what_if_range_columns: Battery size: simulated capacity. Battery profit: total profit over the period. Net bill: calculated bill with the battery. Profit change: difference from the previous size. Profit change per added kWh: that difference divided by the added capacity. The first row has no previous size. Highlighted values are the highest among the displayed results, not necessarily the best investment.
dashboard.what_if_chart_growth_legend: Color shows the average profit change per added kWh in each interval: green is higher, red is lower. Green can also be negative.
dashboard.what_if_interval_color_legend: Green: higher profit per added kWh. Red: lower profit per added kWh among the displayed intervals. Green can also be negative.
dashboard.what_if_interval_explain: The difference between two sizes is the extra profit in the simulated period. Profit per added kWh is that difference divided by the extra capacity. With very small steps the figures can be imprecise.
dashboard.what_if_bill_explain: The calculated bill includes wear and the value of energy left in the battery, and the energy in the battery at the start is a cost; battery purchase cost and fixed fees are excluded.
dashboard.what_if_form_explain: A new calculation uses only the what-if entities here and the current settings. Other values from a saved calculation started by an action or automation are not reused; the entities keep their own values.
dashboard.what_if_empty: Run a simulation to see results.
dashboard.what_if_explain: See what a bigger battery, other charging settings or other rules would have meant with your own history. Fill in only the fields you want to change; the result is shown as a notification. If there is less history than requested, the notification explains why. Results are historical estimates, not an expected saving: the simulation knows the actual consumption and solar production in advance, so real results are usually somewhat lower. Requires administrator access.
dashboard.help_problem:
**A crash or error** (an error notification, *Error* as the charging rule, entities that stay unavailable) **or a wrong decision** (it charged, discharged or sold when it shouldn't have, or didn't when it should - or the charging rule looks wrong):

1. Press **Export debug info** below **as soon as possible** - the file holds the latest calculations and log messages, older ones are replaced as time goes by.
2. A notification appears. Download the file and open the GitHub issue from the link in it (version and time are filled in).
3. Describe what happened and **when** (the time), which rule and battery action were shown, and what you expected instead. A screenshot of the plan helps.
4. Drag the file into the field *Debug file*.

The file is anonymised: no names, passwords, API keys, coordinates or addresses, entity names are replaced. Nothing is sent by itself - you decide what you upload.
dashboard.help_control:
* **Control the battery with the whole period optimisation**: calculates the cheapest action for every hour of the whole forecast period at once (charging loss, wear, solar, buy and sell prices and the profit requirements) and controls the battery with it. Every action is shown as the rule it corresponds to, and the rule switches decide which actions it may use. Off: the rules control the battery.
* **Enhance battery efficiency**: the plan uses the battery's efficiency curves instead of one fixed charging loss. See *Battery efficiency* in the analysis.
* **Learn charging power by battery level**: a battery charges more slowly when it is nearly full. BattMind measures this itself from the battery's power and level (the same measurements as the efficiency) and the plan only counts on the energy the battery takes in each hour; without enough measurements, or off, the charge rate you set is used. The simulator does not use it.
* **Use measured battery capacity**: BattMind always measures how much energy the battery takes and gives per 100 % of level (see *Measured capacity* in the analysis). On: when the charging figure is clearly below the configured capacity, the plan counts on the measured capacity instead, never on more than the configured one; it is not used where a measured efficiency curve is in use (that curve was measured with the configured capacity). Off: the plan uses the configured capacity. The simulator does not use it.
* **Forecast type**: how the consumption per hour is predicted from the history. EMA weights the most recent days highest, trend follows the development, and average weights all days equally.
* **Choose the forecast type automatically**: the plan uses the forecast type that has predicted the consumption best recently and only switches when another is clearly better. See *Forecast accuracy* in the analysis.
* **Correct the price forecast**: the plan corrects the forecast prices (e.g. Carnot) by how far off they usually are. See *Price forecast* in the analysis.
dashboard.help_profit:
Profit thresholds decide when the battery is discharged and when it sells.

* **Min. profit per kWh**: every kWh out of the battery (used in the house or sold) has to earn at least this per kWh after charging loss and wear. Grid charging is only planned when that discharge pays.
* **Min. total profit**: a sale to the grid has to earn at least this in total (per hour; not used for charging or the home's own consumption).
* **Min. excess kWh for export**: smallest amount sold at a time.
* **Reserve for the house**: the battery percentage kept for the home's own consumption and not sold.
* **Exclude sell hours**: hours (e.g. 17,18,19) where nothing is sold.
dashboard.help_charging:
Solar surplus always charges first; grid charging never pushes out solar that would be sold for less than the grid kWh cost.

* **Cheapest hours**: fill the battery in the cheapest hours for the day's consumption (*fill up*: to max).
  * **Cheap price periods**: number of local low-price periods identified per day.
  * **Cheap-period price increase**: how much the price can rise above a period's lowest price before the period ends.
  * **Cheapest-price increase**: how much an hour can be above the day's lowest price and still qualify for this rule.
* **Most expensive hours**: charge for the most expensive hours the battery doesn't cover.
* **Needed before max level**: charge the little that is missing before the sun fills the battery.
* **Negative prices**: fill the battery when charging pays even if the energy is never used.
* **Recommended full charge every**: some LFP batteries need a full charge now and then so the battery management system can calibrate. When more days than this have passed since the battery last reached its maximum level (minus 1 %), BattMind charges it from the grid up towards that level in the cheapest hours before the end of tomorrow (before the end of today once it is a day overdue, also when no full charge is recorded and none is found in the history). It waits until the prices up to that deadline are known, ignores *Min. profit per kWh* and lets the sun charge first. If the battery cannot get there in time, the plan says so and drops the charge. With *Days to plan* of 1 only an overdue full charge is planned. 0 = off.
* **Last full charge**: when the battery last reached its maximum level (minus 1 %); recorded also while the number is 0.
dashboard.help_discharging:
* **Profit only**: block discharging in hours where the battery's kWh cost (incl. loss and wear) is higher than the price.
* **Prioritise expensive hours**: save the battery for the most expensive hours until it is charged again.
* **Before the sun**: use/sell the battery before the sun when it gets full of solar anyway and the surplus is sold cheaply.
* **Max. hours old kWh**: energy older than this is used even without profit, and sold when that pays more.
dashboard.help_selling:
* **Maximise profit**: sell in the most expensive periods when that pays more than using the energy yourself.
* **Sell excess kWh**: sell the energy that isn't used before the battery is empty or full again.
* **Use midnight battery level**: only look until midnight instead of the whole forecast period.
* **Buy to sell**: charge cheaply from the grid only to sell the kWh again when it pays after loss and wear.
dashboard.help_solar:
* **Solar charging**: include the solar surplus in the plan.
* **Optimise solar charging**: sell the solar surplus in the expensive hours and fill the battery in the cheap solar hours instead. Only when the sun will still fill the battery later.
dashboard.price_check_none: No result. It is made with every price update.
dashboard.price_check_legend: ✅ passed · ❌ failed · ➖ not judged or not tested (not a pass) · 🧪 not confirmed
dashboard.price_check_report: Have you seen a provider work with your real data, with the right amounts? Report it on GitHub:
dashboard.help_price_check:
With every price update each chosen price provider is tested on its own prices: whether it gives the prices the plan needs. It only reports: no price and no plan depends on it, and a pass does not say that the amounts are right.

* **Confirmed in your country**: someone has seen the provider work with real data there. A test never changes it.
* **Overall**: ✅ only when the unit, the buy prices of today and tomorrow and the sell prices have passed. Octopus Energy without an export tariff needs no sell prices.
* **Unit**: the unit of the price sensors is read correctly.
* **Buy and sell prices**: complete from the current hour to the end of today, and for tomorrow.
* **Forecast, days after today**: how far the forecast reaches.

➖ means it can't be judged or is not tested, for example tomorrow's prices before 20:00, a sensor that is unavailable, or a provider with no sell sensor and no sell prices. In a market without published prices for the next day, tomorrow shows ❌ in the evening.

At the bottom of this section is the link *Price Provider Verification Report (Confirmed)*. Use it when you have seen a provider work with real data and the amounts are right. It opens a new public issue on GitHub, filled in with the providers, the country, the versions and the results of this check, but no sensor names, prices or other data of yours. Clicking the link sends these fields to GitHub; nothing is published until you submit the issue there, and a report does not confirm a provider by itself.
dashboard.help_automation_test:
BattMind never controls your battery: your own automation does, when BattMind's action changes. This test checks that the automation really does what each action should.

* **Test my automation**: turn it on to start. BattMind publishes the actions one after the other (Charge from grid, Forced discharge, Discharge allowed, Solar charging only, Solar charging blocked, Stop battery) and measures the battery. A step passes as soon as the battery has shown what it should do, and waits at most 5 minutes. Turn the switch off to stop; BattMind's own action is then published again.
* **Automation test**: the status of the test: idle, running, done, stopped or failed.
* The table below lists every action from the start and shows how far the test is (⏳ waiting, ▶️ testing now); each action gets its result when it is done: ✅ worked, ❌ the battery did not react, 🔧 not tested. Actions that depend on the sun or the house load can only be proven when the conditions are right (e.g. the action that blocks solar charging needs a solar surplus), so they are shown as not tested, with the reason, instead of passing. *Stop battery* is the safety stop for a battery temperature that is too high, too low or unknown: without a temperature sensor BattMind never sends it, so it needs no steps. It is tested last: a stop can only be proven by a change, so when the battery stands still the test first makes it move (it publishes *Forced discharge*, or *Charge from grid*, for a short time). Click *Show the test result* to see the table; it is open while the test runs.

**Be aware:** the test charges the battery from the grid and discharges it to the grid for a few minutes, and it changes what the inverter does. Nothing is tested while the battery is stopped for temperature, and the plan and the settings are not changed. Energy the test moves is counted like any other energy in the history of the hour.
dashboard.economy_intro: Per month from the charging history:
dashboard.no_data_yet: Collected from now on: the first figures after a day.
dashboard.economy_explain:
What the battery earned per month, from the charging history.

* **Charged (☀️)**: kWh into the battery, in brackets the part from solar.
* **Charge price**: what a kWh in the battery cost (grid at the buy price, solar at the sell price it would otherwise have earned).
* **Discharged**: kWh out of the battery.
* **Value**: what a discharged kWh was worth: the energy the house did not have to buy, plus sales.
* **Margin/kWh**: value minus charge price, i.e. the margin per kWh before loss and wear. The bigger, the better the battery moves energy from cheap to expensive hours.
* **Avg. price**: the month's average buy price over all hours (from the price sensor's long-term statistics and from now on BattMind's own prices), to compare with the charge price and the value.
* **Savings**: the value of the discharges minus what the energy in the battery cost incl. loss and wear.
dashboard.rules_explain: Charging per rule: **est. gain** = the charged kWh after loss, valued like the battery's discharges on average, minus their price and wear. Discharging per rule: the actual savings. Both tables show the same money from two sides, do not add them up. Days that only exist as one combined entry (for example imported history) are split equally between the rules used that day.
dashboard.cycles_explain: One cycle = discharged kWh equal to the battery size. **Wear** = the wear cost per kWh × charged kWh. The savings are already after loss and wear.
dashboard.loss_explain: Measured loss is the share of the energy that is lost when the battery is charged and discharged, measured with the battery's power sensor. Changes in the battery level are taken into account, so days that empty or fill the battery do not give a loss that is too high or too low. Only whole days with enough charging count. A day whose loss is far from the other days' is left out and counted under **Outliers**. Shown once at least one battery size has been charged. **Used now** is the loss BattMind plans with.
dashboard.efficiency_curve_explain: The efficiency of charging and discharging at different power levels (how much of the energy ends up in the battery or in the house). BattMind measures it itself from the battery's power and level, and reads the first measurements from Home Assistant's history so the curve does not have to wait for new data. The dashed lines are the measured values; the solid lines are the curve BattMind plans with. A curve you set yourself takes precedence over the measured one. If *Enhance battery efficiency* is off, or there is no curve yet, BattMind uses the round-trip loss. A wrong battery size shifts charging and discharging in opposite directions, but the total loss stays correct. Below the efficiency table, *Measured capacity* shows what the battery's power sensor saw per 100 % of battery level over runs of at least 40 % of level: charging gives an upper bound of the usable capacity and discharging a lower bound, because the efficiency is not known. The two are kept apart, and the round trip is their ratio. If the battery level follows the energy evenly, a charging figure clearly below the configured capacity suggests that the usable capacity is smaller, and a discharging figure clearly above it that it is larger. If more energy comes out than goes in per point, that points to a measurement problem (the sensor measures the two directions differently, or the level does not follow the energy evenly). It is always measured. With the switch *Use measured battery capacity* (*Settings → Control*) on, the plan counts on the measured capacity when the charging figure is clearly below the configured capacity, never on more than the configured one, and not where a measured efficiency curve is in use (it was measured with the configured capacity and already follows the battery, so changing the capacity as well would correct twice). *Used now* shows what the plan counts on.
dashboard.efficiency_curve_off: The efficiency curves are turned off. BattMind currently uses the round-trip loss; the configured curves are still saved, and the measurements continue and remain visible.
dashboard.capacity_note: Always measured. The plan only counts on it with the switch *Use measured battery capacity*, and only when the measurement is clearly below the configured capacity.
dashboard.capacity_status_too_few: Not enough runs of at least 40 % of battery level yet (3 of each direction are needed).
dashboard.capacity_status_within: The measurements do not contradict the configured capacity.
dashboard.capacity_status_below: Charging took less than the configured capacity per 100 % of level: the usable capacity looks smaller than configured.
dashboard.capacity_status_above: Discharging gave more than the configured capacity per 100 % of level: the usable capacity looks larger than configured.
dashboard.capacity_status_inconsistent: More energy came out than went in per percentage point. The battery power sensor may measure the two directions differently, or the battery level may not follow the energy evenly.
dashboard.capacity_off: The plan uses the configured capacity: *Use measured battery capacity* is off. The measuring goes on.
dashboard.capacity_source_efficiency: configured: a measured efficiency curve is in use (measured with the configured capacity)
dashboard.forecast_intro: Error of the consumption forecast per hour in kWh
dashboard.forecast_better: ⭐ {best} was the most accurate the last 30 days: on average {best_mae} kWh off per hour against {selected_mae} kWh for the selected ✅ {selected} ({percent} % less error). The actual consumption was {actual} kWh per hour; {best} expected {best_forecast} kWh and {selected} {selected_forecast} kWh. The forecast type can be chosen under Settings → Forecast type, or turn on *Choose the forecast type automatically*.
dashboard.forecast_auto_on: 🔄 The plan chooses the forecast type automatically and now uses ✅ {selected}, the most accurate the last 30 days. It only switches when another type has at least 5 % less error, so it does not jump back and forth between nearly equal types.
dashboard.forecast_auto_waiting: 🔄 The automatic choice of the forecast type starts after {days} days of measurements. Until then the plan uses the selected ✅ {manual}.
dashboard.forecast_title: Average error per hour and day
dashboard.forecast_explain: The average error per hour between the consumption the plan expected and the measured consumption (without battery charging and ignored consumption). ✅ is the forecast type the plan uses, ⭐ the most accurate one the last 30 days. **Bias** > 0: the plan expected too much. **Avg. kWh/hour** is the consumption each type expected on average, against the actual consumption at the top. With *Choose the forecast type automatically* on, the plan itself uses the most accurate type and only switches when another is clearly better. Otherwise the forecast type you selected is used.
dashboard.score_intro_2: of the possible savings the last 30 days
dashboard.score_explain: Shows how much of the possible saving was reached. **Possible** is what the battery could have saved that day, calculated afterwards: the cost without the battery minus the lowest possible cost with the day's actual consumption, solar and prices, losses, wear and the profit requirements, and the battery ending the day where it started. **Saved** is possible minus what the plan lost against the best plan that nets the same battery energy as the day did, so energy kept in the battery for tomorrow, or used from yesterday, is neither a gain nor a loss. Energy that ignored consumers and Cable Juice Planner chargers took from the sun or the battery, and the battery's own standby use, are not part of the score. A day only gets a score when every hour is measured, with real prices and a measured battery level; the days without a score, and why, are listed below the table. A day with very little possible saving shows – instead of a score. Forecast errors are included. A day scored with an older version of the calculation is shown with 🔄 by the formula of then, and is not included in the 30 day figure.
dashboard.score_missing_intro: Days without a score in the last 30 days:
dashboard.score_no_drift: the energy did not add up
dashboard.score_no_battery: the battery could not be modelled
dashboard.score_no_history: an older day without hourly data
dashboard.score_no_version: a day recorded by an older version
dashboard.score_old_note: 🔄 = calculated with an older version of the score. It cannot be compared with the newer days and is not included in the 30 day figure.
dashboard.planned_title: Planned the evening before against actual
dashboard.expensive_intro_1: Empty battery in the most expensive hours on
dashboard.expensive_explain: The day's 4 most expensive hours where the battery was empty (at most 2 % above the minimum) and the house bought from the grid. kWh and {valuta} are the energy bought in those hours.
dashboard.solar_forecast_intro: Planned solar surplus (the evening before) against the measured surplus per day:
dashboard.price_forecast_intro: The price integration's forecast against the real price, the last 30 days:
dashboard.price_forecast_no_data: Collected from now on: the first figures tomorrow at 13:00, when the real prices for the following day arrive.
dashboard.price_forecast_unit: Error and bias in {valuta_kwh}. In brackets: the extra price per kWh of picking the hours by the forecast.
dashboard.price_forecast_explain: Every hour BattMind saves the buy price from the price integration's forecast (without BattMind's own adder per day ahead) for the coming days. When the real prices of a day arrive (around 13:00 the day before), they are compared with what the forecast said 1, 2, 3 … days before. **Error** is the average deviation per hour, **Bias** > 0: the forecast was too high. **Cheapest found**: how many of the day's 4 cheapest hours by the forecast really were among the 4 cheapest (where the plan charges). The extra price in brackets is what picking by the forecast instead of the real hours cost per kWh. The chart shows the real prices and the forecasts of the last and the coming days. **Correction**: with *Correct the price forecast* on, the plan adjusts the forecast prices by their usual error for that many days ahead (at most ±0.50 {valuta_kwh}). The chart then also shows the corrected forecast the plan uses.
dashboard.price_forecast_correction_off: The correction of the price forecast is off (*Settings → Control*).
dashboard.price_forecast_correction_waiting: The forecast is corrected per day ahead after 7 days of measurements.
dashboard.sufficiency_explain: Where the house's consumption came from per hour: first solar, then the battery, the rest from the grid. **Self-sufficiency** = (solar + battery) / consumption. **Export** is solar and battery energy sold to the grid. The first time a year is read from Home Assistant's long-term statistics.
dashboard.planned_explain: Every evening at 23 BattMind saves what the plan wants to charge from the grid and sell the next day. Here it is compared with what was actually charged from the grid and sold. Big differences come from forecast errors (consumption, solar) and from plans that change during the day when the prices or the battery level change.
dashboard.solar_forecast_explain: The solar surplus (solar production minus the house's consumption) the plan expected for the next day, saved the evening before, against the measured surplus. **Plan** is the combined forecast BattMind uses, **History (weather)** is the part from the stored solar history per weather type, **Forecast integration** the solar forecast integration you selected (Solcast, Forecast.Solar or Helios Forecast). **Bias** > 0: too much solar was expected.
dashboard.history_explain:
* **Required battery level until the next charge**: the last 48 hours.
* **kWh charged by solar**: solar energy into the battery, the last 7 days.
dashboard.consumption_forecast_explain: The predicted consumption per hour for the forecast period with the three forecast types (left axis), and the accumulated consumption (right axis, the thick lines). The selected forecast type is used in the plan; **Forecast accuracy** shows which one is most accurate.
dashboard.what_if_inputs_explain:
Run the what-if simulator from entities. The BattMind planner is replayed twice on your own hourly history: once with the current settings and once with the values you change here. Nothing is sent to the inverter and the live plan is not changed.
* **History (days)**: How many days of history are simulated, at most 365.
* **Battery size (kWh)**: The scenario's battery capacity. 0 compares against a home without a battery.
* **Compare a range of battery sizes**: Also simulates several battery sizes; needs the start, end and step below, at most 12 sizes.
* **From (kWh), To (kWh) and Step (kWh)**: The interval. It starts at the start value and includes the end value only when the step reaches it exactly.
* **Compare battery modules**: Also compares what whole extra modules on top of the current capacity give.
* **Module capacity (kWh), Price per module and Additional modules**: The size and price of one module (in the currency of Home Assistant) and how many are added, 1 to 12.
* **Run simulation**: Turn on to start the simulation (one at a time), turn off to stop it. A stopped or failed run keeps the previous result. Progress and errors are shown in the status below, and the result is saved and still shown after a restart.
dashboard.what_if_rules_explain:
By default the scenario uses the current rules and settings. Only values you change are used in the scenario; Current always uses the current ones. The rules and settings are grouped as on the Settings tab.
* **Rules (Charging, Discharging, Control and so on)**: Current keeps the live switch, On or Off changes it in the scenario only.
* **Settings (reserve, minimum profit, minimum total profit, minimum kWh to sell, cheap price periods, rise thresholds and maximum age)**: Unknown uses the current setting; an entered value replaces it in the scenario only.
* **Exclude selling hours**: Hours (0-23, comma-separated) that are not sold in the scenario. Unknown uses the current hours; an empty value means no excluded hours.
* **Reset to current**: Sets all scenario rules and settings back to current.
Rules that need an action the battery cannot run are not shown.
dashboard.what_if_rule_edit_title: Rules and settings in the scenario
dashboard.what_if_rule_note: Values are from the simulation. Enabled rules may be used but did not necessarily execute. A dash means inactive or no battery.
dashboard.what_if_rule_unavailable: Rule values are missing from this saved result. Run the simulation again to see them.
dashboard.what_if_rule_optimizer_control: Control the battery with the whole period optimisation
dashboard.what_if_rule_cheapest_hour_fill_up: Charging: Fill up during cheapest period
dashboard.what_if_rule_needed_before_max_level_pla: Charging: Required before max level planner
dashboard.what_if_rule_force_powerwall_max_hours_o: Forced discharge: Max. kWh age in hours
dashboard.what_if_rule_min_total_profit: Min. total profit (sale to the grid)
dashboard.what_if_rule_powerwall_max_hours_old: Max. age of kWh in home battery
dashboard.what_if_reason_no_recorder: The comparison requires Home Assistant's history (Recorder).
dashboard.what_if_reason_no_buy_price: A buy-price entity is required for the historical what-if comparison.
dashboard.what_if_reason_history_failed: The history in Home Assistant could not be read.
dashboard.what_if_reason_range_incomplete: The capacity interval needs a start, an end and a step.
dashboard.what_if_reason_range_invalid: The capacity interval must use values from 0 to 1000 kWh, a positive step, an end no lower than the start, and at most 12 values.
dashboard.what_if_reason_module_incomplete: The module comparison needs a module capacity and a price.
dashboard.what_if_reason_module_invalid: The module capacity must be above 0 and at most 1000 kWh, the price must not be negative and the number of modules must be from 1 to 12.
dashboard.what_if_reason_invalid_inputs: One of the what-if inputs is not valid or has no value.
dashboard.what_if_reason_save_failed: The result could not be saved.
dashboard.what_if_reason_internal_error: The simulation failed; see the Home Assistant log.
dashboard.help_storm:
BattMind keeps the battery charged for a storm warning from the entity chosen in the settings (MeteoAlarm). Only warnings of wind, snow/ice or thunderstorms at or above the chosen level count, and only warnings that have a start time: without one nothing is planned and the status says so.

* **Storm warning**: the status of the warning. *Coming* or *Active* means the plan keeps a battery level for it. Below it: when the warning starts and ends, the level the battery is kept at, the expected house use with no solar and the buffer added for a forecast that is off (what the forecast missed by over the last 30 days, at least 20 %).
* **Hours a storm warning without an end time covers**: how long a warning is counted when it has a start time but no end time.

The level to keep falls hour by hour as the storm goes on, and nothing is sold under it. Charging is placed in the cheapest hours before the level is needed; if the battery cannot get there in time it is charged as high as it can. Without a backup power supply a full battery does not run the house in a power cut.
